speaker: Speaker 1
words: The following interview is with Elizabeth Mavis taped July 14, 1975 at St. Mary's, Idaho by Dale Anderson. The interview was recorded on July 14, 1975 at St. Mary's, Idaho by Dale Anderson. Could I use your pen? I ran off without mine.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Would you like to sit here? Would this be easier for you? Okay, this one I think works.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, I'll draw you a book. Okay. Okay, first of all, we can start off with personal data. But if there's anything that you really don't want on the tape, just be sure to say that. Okay? And you don't have to answer the question. Oh. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you spell your last name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Capital M-A-B-B-U-T-T.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: U-T-T? Uh-huh. Okay, do you have any nicknames?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, my name is Elizabeth. Most people call me Betty. Betty. Can you see all right there? Main name? Siegel. Capital S-I-E-G-E-L.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: G-E-L? Uh-huh. Date of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: October 19, 1908.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Scottville, Michigan.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Your phone number? I have it with me someplace.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 245- I think it's 2964. I'll find out. Yes, 2964. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Locale of first residence that I know of? Pardon? Locale of first residence that I know of?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh. Well, it's, I guess you'd say Harvey Creek.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Harvey Creek?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: This is not a town. It's not a post office, but that's where we lived.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And where did you live before you moved to Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Michigan.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And the year that you arrived in Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mode of travel? Car.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A Chevrolet Sport Coupe with a rumble seat. There were five of us came out from Michigan.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Who were those five?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My sister, two brothers, and a friend of my sister's. Which meant that two, at least two of us had to ride in the rumble seat out under the sun. You know what a rumble seat is, don't you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think so.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, instead of the car trunk lid lifting this way, it lifted that way, and there was a seat there. Oh. See, so you could, when the back came up and you had a seat back there, but you had no lip over your head.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, did the other people have a lip over their heads, or?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, in the front. Oh. It was like an extra seat in the car, but it was in the trunk compartment, you know. Well, they were all the gold at that time. This was, you know, a very sporty thing. And, well, all five of us wanted to come, and this was the kind of car we had, so that's why we came.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What made you decide to come?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we had relatives visit here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your mother's maiden name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, girl, I have to stop and think. Velker, capital V-O-E-L-K-E-R. It's a German name. V-O. Capital V-O-E-L-K-E-R.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And her first name? Bertha. Date of birth? Her. Oh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it was August 29th, and I can't tell you the year for sure. Let's see. Let's see. Well, let's see. She died in 1968, and she was ‑‑ would have been 89, I think. Oh, no, that's not right. Let's see. She must have been born in 18, probably 1879, I would imagine. I think that's right. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She was born in Michigan.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you're married? Date of birth? 19... 2. Occupations and jobs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My mother's? Well, she spent most of ‑‑ she did some millenary work, I think, before she was married, but no other work outside of that. She raised seven children, and it was quite a job, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can imagine. Your father's name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Arthur Siegel.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: His date of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it was March 13, and I think it would have been probably 1878.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Shatsburg, Michigan.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. S-h-a-s-t?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: S-b-e-r-g, I think. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Date of his death? Death?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: January 2, 1971.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: His occupations and jobs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, gosh, he was a railroad telegrapher, a station agent. Those were the main jobs.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. And all I need now is your brothers and sisters' names.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You want all of them?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: All seven.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay. Muriel M, capital M-u-r-i-e-l, Muriel, Mildred, Donald, Dorothy, Paul, Grant, and, of course, me. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your sisters' married names?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Muriel? Muriel is not married. Mildred is not married. Dorothy is U-I-l-l. Y-u-i-l-l.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's different.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, it is different.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was there any reason your sisters didn't get married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I think they just didn't want to. They were working and had good jobs and very independent, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Your husband's name?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: George Edward.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is he still living? No. Okay. The date of his birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, September 16th. The year, I just cannot remember for sure. Is that important?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, to me, approximately.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Approximately. Well, I should know that, too. Well, let's say 1900. I'll say 1900. That isn't right, I know, but it's...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Place of birth?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, Shoshone, Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Date and place of marriage?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, Spokane, Washington. Oh, let's see. I can tell you. March 15th, 19... Oh, wait a minute. 35.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. And the date of his death?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: May 28th, 1958. May 25th. Excuse me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: 1958? Yes. His occupation for a job?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, he was... Well, a cook was one of the main things. He did a lot of different types of work. But I would say the main thing was cooking.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How'd you meet him?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, gosh. Well, he came in the area where I was to do some work. And there were not many people in the area, you know, so you'd get acquainted. And that's how.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did you know him before you got married? Oh...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A couple of years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What sorts of things did you do during the courtship?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, not very much because we weren't living where there was anything much to do, you know, like places to go or anything. Just visited and took little walks. That's really all there was to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did he go horseback riding or anything like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, didn't have horses. He liked to ride. He was brought up on a ranch and the kids all rode horses. He used to tell me about his sister. She was just a girl, you know, 12, 14 years old. She'd ride her horse down to milk the cow and come back carrying a pail of milk, you know, and holding it out like that and get off her horse without spilling a drop. They had a lot of horses. This was in southern Idaho and they really went for horses down there. But no, we didn't have anything. It was up, you know where Marble Creek is? Marble Creek up the river there? Yeah, it was up there and this was a long time ago, you know. And there was nothing, no place to go, nothing to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that where you were living at the time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, yes. Right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were you doing, Martin, before you got married? Were you working or...?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no, not then I wasn't. I had worked previously but not for a few years because there wasn't anything up there to do, you know, no work.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I didn't have any of my own. I had two stepchildren. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why don't you just give me their names and their occupations?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Dorothy Sword, capital S-W-O-R-D, and she's a housewife. She's not working. And William Mabbeth, his name would be. Well, he works for the BLM, you know what that is? Bureau of Land Management. And I don't just really know what his job is called that he does, but he's worked for them for years. In fact, that's his life work, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Your education?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: High school and about one year of college.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, which good college?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Battle Creek, Michigan. I hear thunder's coming closer again.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. I'm sure it'll be on the tape. It's amazing how much that picks up.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, it is, isn't it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, skills.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mine? Yeah. Oh, I don't have any.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Sure you do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not actually. Well, I did office work, and I can type, you know, and some filing and stuff. Oh, clerical, clerical skills, you might say. I was a bank teller for six years, two, and a waitress for about three.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When were you a bank teller?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That was right before your husband died, right? Mm-hmm. Were you doing that to support both of you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, yes. He wasn't able to work. Let's see. Yeah, that's just about the time that he had to quit work, but I was working as a waitress before that, too, and he was working, and then he had to quit. He couldn't work anymore. So, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Any other jobs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: For me? That's about it. Oh, well, I worked for the employment office for 11 years, which is the state employment office here in St. Mary's, and the last two years I was managing the office.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When did you do that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When? 1959 to 1970. 11 years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you just recently retired from that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, almost five years ago.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. Your interests, hobbies, and talents?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Talents I have none. My interests? Oh, I love to read. I love to work crossword puzzles, jigsaw puzzles, garden. Travel. I love to travel.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where do you travel?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I've been to Alaska, I've been to Hawaii, I've been to Yucatan in Mexico, you know, and the Baja Peninsula, that's in Mexico, you know, it's just south of California, you know where that is.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you go with your husband?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no. I went with my sister. Yeah, went with this one sister. My sister Mildred, we went to all those places. And then, of course, I've been, had a lot of trips just around the United States, different places.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Which place did you like the best?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's very difficult to say. I loved them all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you think of Alaska? Did you go during the summer?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mm-hmm. Well, I liked Alaska. This had been one of my dreams, was to see Alaska. This is, you know, the thing that you dream about the time you're a kid, you know, to see Alaska. So we finally decided to go, and actually, this amazes me, because I'm not usually disappointed in anything, but I was disappointed in Alaska. People are not giving a true picture of Alaska, it seems to me. Have you been there?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: My husband has, but I haven't.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I always thought of Alaska as having great big beautiful timber and beautiful rushing clear streams with a lot of fish in them, you know, and beautiful mountains. Well, the mountains are beautiful. I was not disappointed in the mountains. But the streams, even where they're big, they're just filled with this glacial silt. They're muddy looking. They're not pretty.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you fish? No. Did you go fishing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. I guess there is good fishing, but we didn't go fishing, because we don't, either one of us, care to fish. And then the timber, you know, just a little bit of this stuff. And of course, when you understand the reason why, it's because of the permafrost, you know, is right below the soil about, well, some places the soil will be that deep, you know, fog soil that they can plant things, things can grow, but right under that is solid frozen. Therefore, the trees don't get, have enough root system to grow big and beautiful. They just grow a little and spindly, and then when there's a storm or anything to wash the roots, well, they tip. We saw so many trees, these little trees tipping, you know. Finally, we asked somebody, why was that? So they explained to us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We went camping over the 4th of July up on Bustle Creek. Yeah. And the area where we were had some really big cypress trees.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Cypress?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, cedar. Cedar. Cedar. Cedar trees. And I was just amazed, because those were the biggest trees I've seen in Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There are some big cedars. Well, see, we homesteaded, now you said Bustle Creek, and we homesteaded at Dividual Creek. You know where Dividual Creek is? Let's see, if I had a map I could show you, but it's almost in more or less the same area. And there was a great big cedar, where there was a swampy area. The people told us this was a bear wallow, because they like to wallow where there's, you know, water. And these were great big beautiful cedars. They always call them the big cedars, you know, when they're telling you about the trip. We went this far and that far, and we got to the big cedars, you know. So I know that they do grow pretty big up in that area. They're a beautiful tree, aren't they?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was so impressed, because I've seen just barely little trees here, and I'm used to seeing fairly large-sized oaks occasionally.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Whereabouts did you come from? Georgia. Oh, big trees there. Oak trees?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The oak trees are big.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, they are big trees.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Everything's really impressive. When did you homestead?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, this was in 1930. Now, that was, we came out here the summer of 1930, the five of us, in that sport coop. And my brother and I, Paul, we stayed. We didn't go back. And I had intended to go back, you know, just came out for the summer, but we decided to stay and homestead. I never got back to Michigan for 29 years. I'll tell you, here our trees grow tall, you know. I was born in Michigan, lived there until I was 21 years old, and it's a beautiful state, just beautiful. So many lakes, you know, and lots of timber, and it all looked pretty good to me. But I flew back there, and as we were approaching, I went to Detroit. As I was approaching, we were approaching the airport. I looked down, and I saw these bushes. I said, well, what kind of bushes are those? I wondered, because they hadn't been in Michigan for 29 years. I kind of forgot things. And it was until we got in the car and started driving away that I realized those weren't bushes, they were trees. Because, you see, our trees grow so tall. And that's what one of my sisters that's lived in, stayed in Michigan, lived there all the time. She'd been out to visit a number of times. She said, well, that's the first thing I always notice when I come here to visit is how tall the trees are, because they're not like that back there. And I thought they were bushes. Actually, I did at first.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What made you stay here?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, my brother had been working awfully hard, and the summer before, he had broken down his arches. And we'd gone together to school in Michigan, and he had been working as a waiter, and it was very hard on his feet. And everybody wanted him to stay. They thought it would be good for him to spend a year in this country, where there weren't any sidewalks or anything. Just walking on the ground would be the best thing for his feet. And this was when depression was just starting, you know. And we were afraid if we went back, we would not, probably might not have our jobs that we'd had the year before, and this was a distinct possibility that we wouldn't have. And, of course, we didn't have any money, so we depended on the job. Well, we kept hearing people tell about homesteading. You know, you could live on this land for three years, seven months a year for three years, and then you get title to it, 160 acres of timberland. So we thought, well, this would be a good way to spend three years. There wasn't any work anyway to find any place, and maybe the timber would be worth something someday. So that's what we did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you build a house?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes, we built a house. We had a nice cabin built there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Who built it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Log cabin. Well, there was an old-timer around here, and it wouldn't mean anything to you. His name was John Stanfell. He was a carpenter, but he was, he liked the woods, and he always, he had a cabin down near Marble Creek. And so he went up and built the cabin. My dad helped him, and so we got the cabin built. It's still standing up there, too. Oh. Yeah. We sold the timber, and naturally the cabin went along with it, and the people were very happy. It was well built, very well built cabins, 30. So that's what we decided to do. And we did finally sell it and make pretty fair out of it, but it took a long time. It took a lot longer than three years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you farm during that time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, there was no farming country around there. Well, my folks were living, see, they were living at Marble Creek. They lived at several places, but that's as close as I can come to tell you. They were living at Marble Creek, and so we, my brother worked in the summers. We'd come down summers, and he would work, and then we went up there and lived in the winter. So you're supposed to live up there seven months out of the year. So that's what we did. Live up there in the middle of the forest, and not a soul for six or seven miles.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let me finish doing this, then we can continue with that. Clubs, groups, and societies did you belong to?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Clubs, societies? Oh, I don't think he belonged to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That you belonged to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That I do belong to now?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, or any that you belonged to for a long length of time in the past.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I belonged to PEO Sisterhood.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: PEO? PEO. What does that stand for?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, that is a secret.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You don't tell anybody. I've had people tell me a lot of different things that it stands for, but none of them are right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I belonged to a small church, a circle group, Bible study group. And I belonged to, there was lightning flash, I belonged to the Senior Citizen Center down here. And that's all I belonged to and that's all I had time for.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. And awards, honors, and ribbons?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, nothing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you ever endured anything in accounting for your...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no. I don't do handwork.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, right.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Don't sew, don't do handwork. Don't do anything, period. Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What are some of the advantages and disadvantages of living in a rural area?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, you get to know people. Like in a small town like this, walk down the street, you can speak to practically everybody. You know them. And I like that. I think it's very nice.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Anything else?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you're more, you're closer to nature in a small town than you are in a city. In fact, I don't really know what other advantages there are. There are a lot of disadvantages, too. Because you have to go so far. If you want to see anything, go to a show or anything, you have to go so far.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you rather live in a large city?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I never have wanted to, but as I get older, I think maybe I might. It'd be easier to go places, you know?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How big is Battle Creek?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I don't know how big it is now. It was about 30,000, I think, when... Did I mention Battle Creek?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You mentioned when school was...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah, it was about 30,000 at that time, but I expect probably twice that much now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you like it there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I enjoyed that year, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And then, was that right after that that you came to Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right after that. As soon as school was out, we hopped in the car and headed west.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your parents expect you to go to college?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, we always figured you'd finish college. All my brothers and sisters did, let's see. One sister only went two years. They could go two years in and teach. She went to a teacher's college and then she taught. Then she got married, so she didn't go back. And one brother just had one year. Hi. Can you tell us where Earl Weaver lived? Earl Weaver?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where's the Smith's House in the corner? Thank you. You bet.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But my other two brothers finished college, and my other two sisters finished college. I had the least of any of them. I had just one year. It wasn't a full year either, but it added up to about a year in credits that I had.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were your parents, when you were going to school, living in Michigan or they came back?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh, no, they were out here then. They had just come out here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they were living on Marble Creek, is that right?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, or Harvey Creek. Harvey Creek is about two or three miles up past Marble Creek. And there's nothing there except just the creek. There isn't much of Marble except just the creek. You know, you've been up there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, we went fishing on... No, I guess it was on Vessel Creek that we went fishing. Vessel Creek. But last year we were fishing on Marble Creek.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh. Well, you were probably... Now, what I'm speaking of is Marble Creek Station. There used to be a little railroad building there. It was just a flag stop. But they had a little building there that people could wait in. And there was an old one of those old caboose stoves, you know, round. They kept some fuel in there so people were waiting for the train. In winter they could keep warm. Well, they called that the Marble Creek Station and there was a store there. And a place to... you could rent rooms. Was there a problem with the station? No, no. They didn't have anybody renting the station. The building was just there and the section men kept it supplied with wood or coal. Because there were passenger trains at that time. But Marble Creek itself, of course, it comes into the St. Joe River, you know, right up there. And it's a little ways past the station where the station... So when I say Marble Creek, I'm speaking more of the station than I am of the creek itself. But at Harvey there was nothing. When we lived there, it was just the one cabin that we lived in. We just lived there the one summer. And then we moved down to Pocono, which is a mile below Marble Creek. And it's a railroad station too. And then we lived back up at Marble Creek. See, we just went back and forth until finally my dad bought some land and built the house. And that's where my two sisters are now living. They worked in Michigan and Wisconsin until they were... until they could retire. Then they came out here. By that time, my folks were getting where they needed some help, you know. They wanted to stay in their own homes. So my sisters retired, and it's a beautiful country, a lovely place to live. So now my folks are gone, my sisters are still living there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your folks lived a long time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, my mother was about 88 or 89, and my dad was 90... I think he would have been 92 if he'd lived just a couple more months. So they're pretty good to age. And lucky that they could live in their own home and not have to go to a nursing home. You know, this is... I think it's sad when people have to leave their own homes. So they were lucky. They're helpful so that the girls could take care of them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So what now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, it was wonderful. We're all very thankful that it worked out that way.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you and your brothers and sisters do for recreation when you were growing up? Movies.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Movies were a big thing at that time, you know. In fact, movies were just starting when I was just a little kid. Oh, four or five years old, I think. We had a movie theater, and we used to go every Saturday afternoon and watch the serial, you know, Perils of Pauline. Have you ever heard of that? Yes. When they speak of the old time, well, we saw those. And of course, they'd always... You've seen how the old time movies were jerky and all this, and no sound, you know. They just put the words on the screen. But what I remember best is that all those... Well, one time they ended up, they tied Pauline to the railroad tracks when the train was coming. And then that would be the end of the serial for that week, see. So you had to go the next week to see what was... happened to Pauline, poor Pauline.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Got left on the railroad tracks for a week.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, she did. Cost us a nickel, I remember, to go. Nickel piece. It was a lot of money in those days, but... We... We went to the movies. Well, of course, as we grew older... Now, I never did go to dance as much. In fact, none of my brothers and sisters went to the dance as much. But there wasn't really much else. There was no television, you know. We played cards. And... Well, that's about it. Go for rides, drives around the country. That's all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you and your husband do for recreation right after you got married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, golly. No, we didn't have any recreation. Now, this was right in the Depression time, too. There was a movie theater. Got to go occasionally, but... Money was pretty tight, so...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Who did your husband cook for? Pardon? Who did your husband cook for? You said he was a cook.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, he cooked in restaurants, different ones. Here and there, sheep camps and... Forest service camps and, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you travel a lot then? No. No. Well, I mean, did you live in different places or not?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. No, we were in Shoshone and then we came up here. But at that time, there was a place across the river from where my folks lived and it was coming up for sale. And my husband had been brought up on a farm and he thought he would just love to have a little place like that. So we bought that so we could be near the folks because I was the only one out here, the only child out here. You see, the rest of them were all back in Michigan, so the folks kind of wanted us to have the place and we thought it would be fine, so we did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did you stay there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, we stayed there about seven or eight years. Until? When did you come back? Pardon? When we came to town, came to St. Mary's. Well, you see, about that time, he had diabetes and he was very sick at first. Well, very sick the first year and then just in really poor health after that. So, but we stuck it out there for a few years and then he came to town, they asked him to come in and cook for a while at one of the restaurants, so he did. And while he was gone, the house burned down. I was all alone up there and the house burned down. So we didn't have any place to stay, but he was working, so I came to town. Been here ever since.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Would you rather live in town or out there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I loved it up there, just really loved it. Yeah, I'd rather live up there, I think. But it wasn't, I kept our place for about 20 years and I always thought I'd go back someday, but it was unimproved, you know, it would have taken a lot of money to fix it up and everything and I knew I couldn't do it. I couldn't live up there alone anyway, too isolated. Yeah. So it's different, I can live isolated if I've got at least one person with me, but you know, to live all alone that way, no, I knew I couldn't do that for years and years, so I finally sold the place.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You know, this is a hard question to answer.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Why does anybody get married? You just, I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you planning, I mean, did you see in your future when you were younger that you would be getting married? Or is that just something that...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not particularly, I never particularly, you know, like a lot of girls, this is what they want to do, or they know that this is what they want to do, but I didn't know, I never figured that. I always kind of figured I was going to teach school, see, be a school teacher. That's what I always planned to do, and travel every summer. But that's one of the things that didn't quite work out.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Because you came out here? Did you ever want to go back to school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yeah, I almost did a time or two, but, well, just reasons that I didn't. I finally decided not to.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So... And your husband had been married before? Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He had these two children. They were 13 and 16 years old when we got married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you really didn't raise, do you remember raising them?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no, not... no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was there any particular reason why you decided not to have children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, just didn't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. What did you expect out of marriage?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, companionship in your own home, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And were those expectations met?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh yes, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. What were some of the adjustments that you made to being a widow?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Some of the adjustments?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I really don't know. Just being alone is different. Just being alone when you... You're used to living with somebody for years and years, and then all of a sudden you're alone.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's the only adjustment, because I was already working and supporting myself. So there was no adjustment to make there. But it's just to being alone, that's... Having to make all the decisions. And when you went somewhere, you know, I remember the first time I got in the car and went, drove up to see my folks, all alone, it was an awful feeling, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm. Did you make any... Or did you have any expectations for your stepchildren?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your husband have any?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not in particular.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did they go on to school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Bill went to school. He went, oh... I think maybe a year, I remember for sure. He went after he got out of the service. He was in World War II. After he got out of the service, he went to school. I think it was only a year.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What had more effect on you, the war or the depression?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I think the depression, naturally, because that, you know, it influenced your whole lifestyle and your expectations. And when you're in a depression, you don't know when it's going to end and when things are going to be better.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you ever talk about it now with your friends?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, because not very often. It's mentioned occasionally, but you don't do much talking about it. But anybody that lived through it knows what it was like.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, once you got out here and started the homestead, did it actually have an effect on you then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The depression? Yeah. No, not too much, because I wasn't... There was no work for a woman at all, woman or girl. There was no work for me. My father and brother worked on the section. That was about the only work there was for the first couple of years, and then they worked for the Forest Service in the summers after that. And after my brothers went back, started going back to Michigan to go to school, they came out every summer and worked until they were through school. They worked for the Forest Service.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you have a garden at that time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Our first years here, we didn't have a garden because there was no place to have one, but then we did a lot about in 1933. Yeah. Summer of 1933, we finally had a garden spot, and we raised the garden. Then after that, we pretty much were where we could have a garden.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have a garden now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I have a little garden.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you raise any canning?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no. I don't try to raise enough to can. I'm not particularly interested in canning. I did a lot of it, but I don't really enjoy it, see? So now I don't have to do it, and I don't do it. But I freeze a few things. I have a lot of raspberries. I usually have a freezer full of raspberries.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's nice.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it is only after four weeks. After six or eight or ten or twelve years, you get a little... I don't say tired of them. I still enjoy them, but I don't... I wish I didn't have so many, so I'm cutting down my raspberry patch. Do you know about raspberry patches? If you don't watch them, they grow. They grow like this, see? And before I knew it, I had a huge raspberry patch, and I can't believe the weight. So now I'm cutting them down. I think this year I'm going to have just about right. Plenty to eat in summer and a few for freezing, which I would like to have some.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you freeze vegetables for winter?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, if I have to, but I don't plan on it. But if everything comes at once, you know... I did freeze maybe three little cartons of string beans last summer, and that's all. So you can't really say that it's freezing. This is my first attempt, and it turned out pretty well. But, no, I don't...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You had the children here? Did you do a lot of that sort of thing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I never had the children here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Time, this one...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How long does it run?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, the whole tape is 90 minutes. Oh, 90 minutes. So we probably missed maybe... I got here maybe 15, 20 minutes, I would say. Because I didn't have it on while I was taking the pictures. Yeah. Well, maybe even longer than that. Maybe it's going to learn up. What kind of things do newspapers use as far as you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I take news, U.S. News and World Report, and Red Book and TV Guide, and... Oh, my. Reader's Digest. I just quit. There are two of them, and I just let them drop because I've got more reading that I can keep up with. Let's see, I think that's about it. Newspapers, Spokesman Review, Gazette Record, that's it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What is the Gazette Record?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's our local St. Mary's paper.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is that daily?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, weekly. The Review is daily. Every day of the Sunday.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were some of the most common things that your husband asked you about?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, goodness, that was a long time ago. I couldn't answer that question.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you make big decisions? Was it joint? Or did he make decisions about a job for Stefan himself?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes, he was doing the work. I let him do the making of decisions, sure.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever talk about where you might be traveling to?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, because at that time we didn't have any money for a while. There was no chance of traveling. And I don't think he's particularly interested in traveling. So, no, we didn't even think about traveling. For many years I didn't go anyplace really, here to Spokane and back.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We usually go to go to the movies.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Where do we go? Well, Spokane.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you ever go to Coraline?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have a couple of times, but I don't know. We don't get the advertising from Coraline, so I don't know what's on. Spokane, of course, it's always in the paper.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you usually go with?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm going to turn this light off. Oh! Well, I have some friends that we travel, you know, go places together. And, yeah, that's about it. Two friends, a group usually, that we go places.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Is there anything else you'd like to tell me?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Um, no, I can't think of anything. Told you I didn't have much to say.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Any rural experiences, or living in the world of crick?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What's the name of that other crick?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Harvey Creek. H-A-R-V-E-Y, Harvey Creek.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think you mentioned another one.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, the Vigil Creek was where the homestead was. See?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Divigio?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Divigio. I think it's spelled capital D-A-V-E-G-G-I-O. I think it was named after a man, and I don't know whether that was an Italian name or what. It had been named that long before I came to this country. The only thing that I could tell you that I think is different, the only experience I've had that's different, is when we lived up in that area, before the road was built, before there was a road. Now, when the... You know what the three C camps were? CCC camps, do you know what they were? Well, in the Depression, because there were so many unemployed young people in the cities, they had these camps, different places. Mostly in the west, but I think they probably had some in the east too. But they'd ship these boys out from New York and Chicago and Philadelphia and all these big cities to these camps that were set up in the west, and they were going to do work, forest work, see? And the government paid them so much a month, and so much went to their families. This was for their work. Well, when they put those camps in, then they started building the road up to... Oh, see, when we first came here in 1930, there was a road on the north side of the river, and it went as far as Herrick. And Herrick is about three miles, I think, east of Calder. On the railroad, you see, because these were all railroad places. Because there was no road, and the railroad was the main method of transportation, or walking. And then the three C camps, there was one at Marble Creek, and there was one at Herrick. Then there was one in between Marble Creek and Herrick, and they were working on building the road on this side of the river. Now, how far the road had been on this side of the river, I couldn't say for sure how far up it went. But that is what they did, and then after that, there was road on both sides of the river. Well, this was a very kind of a closed-in community, you might say, up there, because, as I said, there were just a very few people. There were only two other women, besides my mother and I, up there. Mostly it was old, and this was down under here. Mostly it was these old woods, woods workers, you know. And then during the Depression, there was no work for them, so they just lived in little shacks all around. They'd just shack up to find an old place and move in, and stay there because there was no work or anything, and this was a very cheap way to live, you know. And there was no electricity up there. There was no road, no electricity, no mail service. When anybody wanted the mail, they could either walk down to Calder. There was a post office at Calder. From where we lived, it was eight or ten miles for the walk. But there used to be lumberjacks that would go down there, and then they'd bring up the pack sack full of mail for everybody that lived up this way, and drop it off at the places, or else take it to Marble Creek. There's a little store there. So then we wanted the mail, we could go to Marble Creek to see if there was any. But we lived right along the tracks, so usually they'd stop at our place and drop off our mail for us. And that's how we got our mail. Now they get mail up there six days a week, which is wonderful. They have mail service, and they have a road that goes all the way up to Avery. And they have electricity. We didn't have electricity when we first went up there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When did you first have electricity?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I was already living in St. Mary's when they finally got the electricity up there. So I can't say for sure, but it must have been, we came here in 1947, it must have been sometime after that that they put the electricity up there. And that's made a great change of things, having the road and electricity and mail service, of course. With the road they could have the mail service. But otherwise people came in on the train, they had passenger trains, and they would stop at, they had two passenger trains, one was the through one that went fast train, you know. And they would practically never stop, but then they had this little local that would stop any place practically anybody wanted them to. Like when we went to Spokane on the train, we'd have to walk several miles to get to the station. And then flag the train and go to Spokane, but coming back we'd ask the conductor to let us off right at our place and he would do that. So that was no problem. Except that we used to, when we lived two or three miles from the station, we'd have to walk and the train came early, about five o'clock, and, well, anyway, we'd get up about one or two o'clock in the morning and walk to the station and flag the train and get to Spokane. Then unless we stayed in Spokane at night, we wouldn't get back till almost midnight that night, which was quite a long day. So it was a little different. It's much different now. But a lot of people still think it's isolated up there, you know, and they live way back, away from everything, but it's nothing like it was. At our homestead we had to walk, of course, all the way up and all the way back, and the winter and the snow was deep. We had to use snowshoes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where'd you go to school? School?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Where did I go to school?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You went to school in Michigan, right? Yeah. Was there still a problem?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. But there was a family up there with three little girls, and they had to go to Marble Creek. There was no school at Marble Creek, but there was another family living near Herrick that had a lot of children, so there was a school at Herrick. And these three little girls, well, the first month or two, well, the youngest one was too little at that time, the two others were about five and seven years old, and they rode the horse way through the backwoods from Marble Creek down to Herrick to go to school and then back at night, which was pretty good for two little kids like that, you know? Yeah. Then in the winter, though, when they couldn't ride the horse, their mother moved down. They had a little, there was a cabin that they could rent, and they moved down there and stayed during the winter. Then in spring, mother moved back up to Marble Creek, and the little girls rode the horse again.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You're talking about wearing snowshoes. Where were you going?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Talking about going where?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That you had snowshoes. Where were you going?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, back up to our homestead cabin. That's where we used them. Because, you see, well, the trail was about two or three miles, fairly straight along Marble Creek, right along Marble Creek. And then we crossed the creek and had these little suspension bridges, and we crossed the creek. Then we started to climb, and we'd go right straight up. It was a steep climb. I don't know how many miles that was, probably three at least, three and a half maybe. It seemed like ten because you were going up all the time. That's a hard, hard trip. You'd come down a lot faster than you could go up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I know about that. You know. I just don't go up very fast at all.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. But it was lovely. It was beautiful. Oh, we had a lot of problems with bear up there, too. Everybody said to me, they said, oh, you're going to Homestead. You're going to go up and shake hands with a bear. And I, well, I just thought they were kidding, you know. We almost did shake hands with a bear one night. My brother and I were, I think it was the, yeah, it was the first fall we were up there. We heard a bear around the cabin. We'd had a can of salmon one night, and I just set it out on a little stoop in front of the door. I set it out there because where we emptied the cans was a little ways away, and I thought we could empty it in the morning. Pretty soon we heard something, and it was a bear, and he took our cans. Well, a few nights after that, let's see, we had an old dog up there with us, too. And I, this kind of scared me when the bear was coming around the cabin, you know. So when I went to bed at night, of course, we had just kerosene lamps because no electricity. I had some matches, and I put these matches right near my bed where I could get hold of them in a hurry, you know, if I needed it. And, well, my brother had a gun. He could shoot, and he had the gun, was in the living room, and we had two bedrooms just off the living room. And, well, we'd gone to bed and gone to sleep, and the old dog slept out by the stove because up in that country, this was long about in October, I think. It was pretty cold, see, it was pretty high country and cold, so we'd always have fire in the stove, and the old dog liked to sleep there. Well, this night, we'd gone to bed and gone to sleep already, and I heard the awfulest noise in the middle of the night. And then I heard my brother yell, and it scared the daylights out of me because I thought, I thought right away that's the bear, he's come into the house. And he's got my brother cornered, see, and this scared me because here I was, too, you know. And then I heard a shot, and Paul told me afterwards, he said, well, I wasn't scared, but he said I yelled, tried to scare the bear. He said the bear had broken the window, see, he was ready to, whether he actually got in or just broken it and heard the sounds, I don't know. We didn't see any indication that he had come in, but this was pretty scary on a black night, you know. And of course, when I tried to light the matches, well, they broke, you know, when you're in a hurry, how things happen. Finally got it lit, and here was the old dog was under my bed. He was scared. And Paul had put the gun just outside his bedroom door, the living room, and where the bear had broken the window was on the opposite side of the house from where our bedrooms were. That was the lowest window. The bedroom windows were high above the ground, see, the ground was uneven slightly, so this window was low, but those windows were high. Well, that was pretty scary. We had a lot of trouble with the bear breaking in and getting our groceries and eating them and carting them off. Bacon and cans of, we used to get things in sacks, beans and rice and all that stuff, you know. Well, one time we had lots of trouble a number of years. One year when we went away in the spring, we had canned some huckleberries the summer before, and, you know, bears like huckleberries. And our cabin had really, you might say, two stories, and the roof was very steep, a sliding roof like that. So Paul built a little shelf up there, and we put our sugar and our huckleberries and anything else we had we thought the bear might be interested, we put it right up next to the top of the roof. Well, it felt perfectly safe. Even if he got in, he couldn't get those things. The next time we went up there, there was a, instead of breaking the windows and going in, he climbed up on the roof and tore a hole in the roof and got them that way. They're smart. Bears are smart. He must have been able to smell that, you see, even through the roof. And through the cans. I don't know how they could, but he must have, because that's where he headed right for that particular place.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your brother go hunting?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He went hunting, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever have bear meat?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, no, we didn't eat bear meat. He didn't go hunting for bears, but the first summer we were out here, this was after the rest of the family had gone back to Michigan. My brother and I had stayed, and my folks, we were staying with the folks. This was at Harvey Creek. And it was the middle of August, and the bear were coming down. See, in the summer they're up high, but long about the middle of August, they start coming down. The berries are riper or something, I don't know. Anyway, they come down. And this, my mother and I had gone for a walk up the track, because this was the only place there was to walk. We walked up the track. And as we were coming back, we saw my dad and brother just on the porch, just waving at us and pointing down to the river. We looked, and there was a little bear, a young bear, maybe about a year old. So we dashed back to the house, and my dad got the gun, and he shot this little bear. Because, see, we didn't have refrigeration, we didn't have any way to get meat except fresh meat. In the summer they wouldn't kill deer. But this bear, well, anyway, he shot him. Oh, the meat smelled awfully good. It smelled like roast pork. And we hadn't had meat for a while, so it was going to taste pretty good. But after my dad skimmed out this little bear, he had the carcasses hanging up there, we looked at it. And you know, it looked for all the world like a baby, a young child hanging there with the feet, you know, and everything. And we couldn't, Paul and I couldn't eat any of that bear meat.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your parents?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, they did. Sure. They were glad to have the bear meat. And of course, summer we couldn't keep it, so we gave the meat to, you know, what we couldn't give to other people. But I've never been able to eat bear meat. I just feel like you're eating something human.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I've heard about that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Have you heard?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: A friend of ours caught a bear, but he was skinning it when I saw it. Oh. So I didn't see it was hanging and then it fell down. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, they don't look so much like it, so much with the skin on, but when you take the hide off, the fur off, why?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did they still have those logging camps on the creek there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They, well, see, because of the Depression, there was no logging, practically no logging, so.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were the camps there? What had been?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There were camps, deserted logging camps, yeah, up where we were homesteading. There weren't any down along the river, but back up there, there was great big camps, well, I've forgotten the names of them now, but Weyerhaeuser and like that, they had camps, big logging companies, you know, had camps, and they were all abandoned, and this was one thing, that there were so much stuff that they didn't move out because it had to be taken out on pack trains, you know, and it would cost them more to move the stuff out than just to leave it there, so they just left it there, so anybody who wanted could go there and get stuff. Well, we got most of the dishes that we used up in our homestead cabin, we got there, there was, oh, I suppose there were enamel dishes, camp, you know, that they used for the men and the cops and like that. We got the dishes, and then after the bear broke so many of our windows, we had to go and get windows from over there, too. That was quite, we had quite a time keeping supplies of windows for a while.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was it hard to get glass?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We could have gotten it, but see, living where we did, it's very difficult, because I suppose there were places in St. Mary's where you could get it, but we would have to come down here, and the way the trains ran, it was very difficult, you know, to get into town to order things. We used to order our groceries by, Burgundy's, have you ever heard of them? It's a furniture store in Spokane now, but way back then they had a grocery store, and they used to send out catalogs, and a lot of people ordered their groceries that way out of the catalog. So we ordered the groceries once or twice a year. We'd get one or two big orders a year, you know. First we'd order, we'd put down the list of what we had to have, you know, you have to have sugar and flour and stuff like that, and then we'd put down, as much as our money allowed, the little luxuries, you know. Well, that was a big deal when the grocery order came in, you know. Just like Christmas when you open this box, and oh boy, look at this and this and that, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can't imagine sitting and trying to buy food just twice a year.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it can be done though. You buy in big quantities, see. The sugar came in hundred pound sacks, and a lot of people that live out in the country, rural areas, you know, would buy it that way because it's cheaper anyway, and then of course you're going to need that much. And flour came in sacks, big sacks too, you know. Now people buy little sacks of flour like that, but we bought big sacks, because we'd bake our own bread, you know. It took a lot of flour.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you still bake your own bread?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I bake bread once in a while. I like to, but I don't make it very often. Well, it doesn't take very many bakings to supply me with enough bread to last, you know, one person. I don't eat where they lay me off. I like it, but I just, so many other things that you don't. But I like to bake. I enjoy baking bread. Do you ever make bread?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, once per period. Well, part of June we didn't have homemade bread, but we pretty much had it for a year now.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, well, that's nice.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's just a matter of keeping up with it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. It isn't so hard.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, it's really easy. Yeah. It's just a matter of taking the time. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And getting it going, and, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did electricity make a big difference in your life right away when you first had it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, see, I was down here when we, of course, when I lived in Michigan, we always had electricity. We had an indoor bathroom and everything. That's why it was such a contrast when we came out here and didn't have all these things, you know. But, oh, goodness, yes, I know with my folks, you know, and everything, instead of our radios, we used to have battery radios, you know. Well, your battery will wear out after a while, you know, and then you have to send an order to get more, and it's just kind of inconvenient. But you plug in your electricity and it should go 24 hours a day. But with the battery, we had to sort of pick and choose and make it last as long as possible. And it happened that the most important things of the time, our battery would run out. When Pearl Harbor, the time of Pearl Harbor, we didn't have any. The battery had run out of our radio, and I didn't know about Pearl Harbor until the next morning. And this was a very, you know, very important thing. And when Franklin D. Roosevelt died, I didn't know about that until the next day, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Somebody told us.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But, of course, it doesn't matter. You live anyway whether you know what's happening or not.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What convenience did you appreciate having when you lived in St. Mary's?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, let's see. Did we have a refrigerator? We were renting when we first moved. Well, in fact, we stayed in the house, and the old couple that owned it had gone south for the winter. And so we stayed there and looked after the house. I can't remember. I think we did have a refrigerator. I think a refrigerator would be one of the main things. And now I didn't have an electric stove here for quite a while. But I think an electric stove, well, maybe that's even more important than a refrigerator. I don't know. But if you've ever tried cooking or canning on a wood stove in the hot summer day, or baking bread or anything, you know, it heats the house up terrifically. And, you know, houses don't usually cool off that fast at night either.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you can with a boiling water bath, or did you have a pressure cooker?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I just, I think you call open kettle methods.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Boy, I tell you, you stand there and the perspiration runs down your back and on. Well, it can be done. It can be done, but I think it's nicer when you don't have to. I think about a lot of these kids today that want to go back and live in the sticks, and I hope they only want to do it for a few years. For a couple of years I think it'd be, it's not a bad experience for them, but I hope they don't intend to always live that way because, well, it's a good experience, but I don't think it's anything to do voluntarily for your whole life. Why should you when you can have it so much nicer, comfortable? You know what I mean? The hippies go back and they don't care if they have any electricity or anything. Well, while you're young, it's kind of a lark and you can manage, but as you get older I think you want more comforts. They seem more important.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, they seem pretty important to a lot of young people.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, of course they do to a lot of them, yes, but I'm thinking of the ones that make such a point about they just want to get back to nature and live well like the cavemen did, I guess. I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't think anybody wants to go back quite that far.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I think it would be a good experience just to go back. I would like to know that I could do that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It's a good experience, and I wouldn't take anything for those years that I had, and it wasn't easy either. Those were some of the most wonderful years of my life, even though they were hard and very inconvenient, and you didn't go much of any place, but you're happy anyway.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What made you happy, dear?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I loved the outdoors, and that was beautiful, beautiful country. Beautiful country. Beautiful, free. I liked the outdoors, and I had a lot of it, and I liked to walk. I still walk around town a lot.
